o: pregio Motezuma il servizio di lui, e tornò ad accordargli la libertà; ma rifiutandola egli come innanzi, gli offerì l' impiego luminoso di Tlacatecatl, o sia Generale delle armi Messicane. A ciò rispose coraggiosamente il Tlascallese, che non voleva esser traditore alla sua patria, e che voleva assolutamente morire, purchè fosse nel sacrifizio gladiatorio, che come destinato per li più riguardevoli prigionieri, sarebbe più onorevole per lui. Tre anni si trattenne in Messico questo celebre Generale con una delle sue mogli, che da Tlascalla se n' era andata colà per vivere con lui. Si può credere, che gli stessi Messicani ciò procurassero, acciocchè lor lasciasse una gloriosa posterità, che nobilitasse colla sua prodezza la Corte, ed il regno di Messico. Finalmente vedendo il Re l' ostinazione, con cui rifiutava qualunque partito gli faceva, condiscese alle barbare di lui voglie, e prefisse il giorno del sacrifizio. Otto giorni innanzi cominciarono i Messicani a celebrarlo con balli, e compito il termine, in presenza del Re, della Nobiltà, e d' una immensa folla di Popolo, misero il prigione Tlascallesse legato per un piede nel Temalacatl, o sia pietra grande e rotonda, dove cotali sacrifizj si facevano. Uscirono ad uno ad uno per combattere con esso lui parecchi uomini coraggiosi, de' quali uccise, per quel che dicono, otto, e ne ferì fino a venti, finattantochè cadendo mezzo morto in terra da un forte colpo ricevuto nel capo, lo portarono innanzi all' Idolo di Huitzilopochtli, ed ivi gli aprirono il petto, e gli cavarono il cuore i Sacerdoti, e precipitarono per le scale del tempio il cadavero secondo il rito stabilito. Così finì questo famoso Generale, il cui coraggio, e la cui fedeltà alla sua patria l' avrebbon innalzato alla classe degli Eroi, se regolato si fosse coi lumi della vera religione. [margin: §. 7. Fame nelle Provincie, dell' Imperio, ed opere pubbliche nella Corte.] Nel tempo, in cui si faceva la guerra contro i Tlascallesi, si patì fame in alcune Provincie dell' Imperio Messicano, cagionata dalla siccità di due anni. Consunto tutto il grano, che aveano i particolari, ebbe il Re occasione d' esercitar la sua liberalità: aprì però tutti i suoi granai, e
e: his service, and again granted him liberty; but he refusing it as before, Bk. V. he offered him the illustrious office of Tlacatecatl, or general of the Mexican forces. To this the Tlaxcalan replied courageously that he would not be a traitor to his country, and that he wished absolutely to die, provided it were in the gladiatorial sacrifice, which, being destined for the most distinguished prisoners, would be more honorable for him. This celebrated general remained three years in Mexico with one of his wives, who had gone there from Tlaxcala to live with him. It may be believed that the Mexicans themselves contrived this, so that he might leave them a glorious posterity, which would ennoble by its prowess the court and the kingdom of Mexico. At length the king, seeing the obstinacy with which he refused whatever proposal was made to him, yielded to his barbarous wishes, and fixed the day of the sacrifice. Eight days before, the Mexicans began to celebrate it with dances, and when the term was completed, in the presence of the king, of the nobility, and of an immense crowd of people, they set the Tlaxcalan prisoner, tied by one foot, on the Temalacatl, or great round stone, where such sacrifices were made. There came out one by one, to fight with him, several courageous men, of whom he killed, as they say, eight, and wounded as many as twenty, until, falling half dead to the ground from a violent blow received on the head, he was carried before the idol of Huitzilopochtli, and there the priests opened his breast and tore out his heart, and threw the corpse down the stairs of the temple according to the established rite. So ended this famous general, whose courage and whose loyalty to his country § 7. would have raised him to the class of heroes, had he been guided by Famine in the provinces of the empire, the lights of true religion. and public works at court. At the time when the war against the Tlaxcalans was being waged, a famine was suffered in some provinces of the Mexican empire, caused by a drought of two years. All the grain that private persons had having been consumed, the king had occasion to exercise his liberality; he therefore opened all his granaries, and distributed

o: distribuì fra suoi sudditi tutto il frumentone, che v' era; ma non bastando ciò a rimediare alla loro necessità, permise ad imitazione di Motezuma I., lo andarsene ad altri paesi a procurarsi il loro alimento. L' anno seguente (1505) avendo avuto un' abbondante raccolta, uscirono i Messicani alla guerra contro Quauhtemallan, Provincia distante più di novecento miglia da Messico verso Scirocco. Mentre si faceva questa guerra, cagionata verisimilmente da qualche ostilità fatta da' Quauhtemallesi contro i sudditi della Corona, si terminò in Messico la fabbrica d' un tempio eretto ad onore della Dea Centeotl, la cui solennissima dedicazione fu celebrata co' sacrifizj de' prigionieri fatti in quella guerra. Aveano ancora per questo tempo ampliata la strada sul lago da Chapoltepec a Messico, e rifatto l' acquidotto, che v' era sopra la strada medesima; ma l' allegrezza, che ebbero per la conclusione di sì fatta opera, si turbò dall' incendio della torre d' un altro tempio detto Zomolli cagionato da un fulmine. Gli abitanti di quella parte della Città, che era più discosta da esso tempio, e particolarmente i Tlatelolchi, non essendosi accorti del fulmine, si persuasero, che un tal incendio fosse stato eccitato da' nemici venuti improvvisamente alla Città: onde si misero tosto in armi per difenderla, e corsero in torme verso il tempio. Ebbe un tale sdegno Motezuma per quella inquietudine, persuadendosi, ciò essere stato un mero pretesto de' Tlatelolchi per muover qualche sedizione, (mentre s' era in perpetua diffidenza di loro) che gli privò di tutti gl' impieghi pubblici, che esercitavano, ed anche proibì, che comparissero nella Corte, non bastando allora a distornarlo da una tal risoluzione nè le proteste, che fecero della loro innocenza, ne le preghiere, colle quali imploravano la Real clemenza; ma tosto che si smorzò quel primo fuoco della sua collera, gli restituì a' loro impieghi, ed alla sua grazia. Frattanto si ribellarono alla Corona i Mixtechi, ed i Zapotechi. I principali capi della ribellione, ne' quali si compromisero tutti i Signori d' ambedue le
e: among his subjects all the maize that there was; but this not sufficing to remedy their need, he permitted, in imitation of Moctezuma I, Bk. V. their going off to other countries to procure their sustenance. The following year (1505), having had an abundant harvest, the Mexicans went out to war against Cuauhtemallan, a province more than nine hundred miles distant from Mexico toward the southeast. While this war was in progress, caused probably by some hostility committed by the people of Guatemala against the subjects of the crown, the building of a temple erected in honor of the goddess Centeotl was completed in Mexico, whose most solemn dedication was celebrated with the sacrifices of the prisoners taken in that war. They had also by this time widened the road on the lake from Chapultepec to Mexico, and rebuilt the aqueduct that was upon the same road; but the joy they felt at the completion of so great a work was disturbed by the burning of the tower of another temple, called Zomolli, caused by lightning. The inhabitants of that part of the city which was farther from that temple, and particularly the Tlatelolcas, not having noticed the lightning, persuaded themselves that such a fire had been started by enemies who had come suddenly upon the city; whereupon they at once took up arms to defend it, and ran in crowds toward the temple. Moctezuma conceived such anger at that disturbance, persuading himself that it had been a mere pretext of the Tlatelolcas to stir up some sedition (for there was perpetual distrust of them), that he deprived them of all the public offices they held, and even forbade them to appear at court, neither the protestations they made of their innocence nor the prayers with which they implored the royal clemency then sufficing to turn him from such a resolution; but as soon as that first fire of his wrath died down, he restored them to their offices and to his favor. Meanwhile the Mixtecs and the Zapotecs rebelled against the crown. The principal leaders of the rebellion, to whom had committed themselves all the lords of both nations

Soon after this expedition some dispute or other arose between Dispute between the Huexotzincas and the Huexotzincas and the Cholulans, their neighbors and friends, the Cholulans. and, committing the decision to arms, they fought a pitched battle. The Cholulans, as more practiced in the exercise of religion, of commerce, and of the arts than in that of war, were soon beaten and forced to retire to their city, to which the enemy pursued them, killed some of their people, and burned some of their houses. No sooner had the Huexotzincas obtained such a victory than they repented of it, because of the punishment that threatened them; hence, to avoid it, they sent to King Moctezuma two distinguished persons, called Tolimpanecatl and Tzoncoztli, seeking to justify themselves and to blame the Cholulans. These ambassadors, whether to make the courage of their fellow citizens appear greater or for any other motive, so exaggerated the slaughter of the Cholulans that they made the king believe that all had perished, and that those few who had saved their lives had abandoned the city. Moctezuma, on hearing this report, was exceedingly grieved by it, and feared the vengeance of the god Quetzalcoatl, whose sanctuary, which was among the most celebrated and

Indi fatti venir colà i suddetti Ambasciatori, e tagliate loro l' orecchie, ed il naso, (che era la pena stabilita contro coloro, che dicevano delle bugìe perniciose al pubblico,) gli consegnarono al Generale. Having therefore taken counsel with the two allied kings, he sent to Cholula some persons of his court to inform themselves fully of the whole affair, and having found it very different from what the Huexotzincas had told him, he conceived such indignation at having been deceived by them that he at once dispatched an army, ordering the general to punish them severely if they should not give fitting satisfaction. The Huexotzincas, sensing the storm that was about to burst upon them, came out drawn up in battle array to receive the Mexicans; but the Mexican general advanced toward them to set forth his commission in these words: “Our lord Moctezuma, who has his court in the midst of the water, Nezahualpilli, who commands on the shores of the lake, and Totoquihuatzin, who reigns at the foot of the mountains, order us to tell you that, having learned from your ambassadors that you have ruined Cholula and killed its inhabitants, they have felt the utmost grief, and are compelled to avenge so great an outrage against the venerable sanctuary of Quetzalcoatl.” The Huexotzincas protested that the report of their ambassadors was too exaggerated and false, and that therefore a body so respectable as that of the city of Huexotzinco could not be the author of it, and they offered to satisfy all three kings by the punishment of the guilty. Then, having caused the aforesaid ambassadors to be brought there, and having cut off their ears and nose (which was the penalty established against those who told lies harmful to the public), they handed them over to the general. Thus they avoided the evils of war, which otherwise would have been inevitable.                 § 10. L' anno seguente uscì l' esercito Reale de' Messicani, Tezcucani, e Tepanechi contro la rimota Provincia d' Amatlan. Nel marciare, che fecero per un' altissima montagna, sopravvenne una furiosa tramontana con neve, che fece nell' Esercito una grandissima strage, mentre alcuni, essendo avvezzi ad un clima dolce, ed andando quasi ignudi, morirono di freddo; ed altri furono sopraffatti dagli alberi, che strappò il vento. Del resto dell' esercito, che continuò indebolito il suo viaggio fino ad Amatlan, morì la maggior parte nella battaglia. Queste ed altre calamità aggiunte alla apparizione d' una cometa in quello stesso tempo nel Cielo, misero in gran costernazione tutti que' Popoli. Motezuma, il quale era troppo superstizioso per poter guardar con indifferenza sì fatto

A very great number of prisoners was sacrificed in it, others being reserved for the festival of the Dedication of the Tzompantli, which was, as we shall say elsewhere, a building near the great temple, where the skulls of the victims were kept strung up. § 11. Presages of the war This secular year seems to have passed without war, but in 1507 with the Spaniards. the Mexicans made the expedition against Tzollan and Mictlan, states of the Mixtecs, whose inhabitants fled to the mountains to save themselves, and the Mexicans had no other advantage than that of taking prisoner a few Mixtecs who had remained in their houses. Then they went to subjugate those of Cuauhquechollan who had rebelled, in which war Prince Cuitláhuac, general of the army, displayed his courage. Some brave captains of the Mexicans died in this expedition; but they brought the rebels back under the yoke nonetheless, and took three thousand two hundred prisoners, who were sacrificed, part in the festival Tlacaxipehualiztli, which was held in the second Mexican month, and part at the Dedication of the sanctuary Zomolli, which after the aforementioned fire had been rebuilt with greater magnificence. The following year the royal army of the Mexicans, Texcocans, and Tepanecs marched out against the remote province of Amatlan. As they were marching over a very high mountain, a furious north wind with snow came upon them, which wrought a very great slaughter in the army, for some, being accustomed to a mild climate and going almost naked, died of cold; and others were crushed by the trees that the wind tore up. Of the rest of the army, which continued its journey weakened as far as Amatlan, the greater part died in the battle. These and other calamities, added to the appearance of a comet in the sky at that same time, threw all those peoples into great consternation. Moctezuma, who was too superstitious to be able to regard with indifference such

o: fenomeno, consultò sopra ciò i suoi Astrologi; ma non sapendo questi indovinarne la significazione, la richiese dal Re d' Acolhuacan, ch' era ancora portato per l' Astrologìa, e la Divinazione. Questi Re, avvegnachè parenti fossero fra loro, e perpetuamente alleati, non però viveano in molta armonìa, dacchè il Re d' Acolhuacan fece morire, siccome fra poco vedremo, il suo figliuolo Huexotzincatzin, non curando le preghiere di Motezuma, il quale come Zio di quel Principe, s' interpose per lui. Era già molto tempo, che non si trattavano più con quella frequenza, e con quella confidenza con cui solevano; ma questa volta il vano terrore, che ingombrò l' animo di Motezuma lo spinse a prevalersi della scienza del Re Nezahualpilli: onde lo pregò di portarsi a Messico per deliberare insieme sopra tal affare, che premeva del pari a tutti e due. Andò Nezahualpilli, e dopo aver conferito prolissamente con Motezuma, fu di parere, per quel che dicono gli Storici, che la Cometa annunziava le future disgrazie di que' regni per l' arrivo di nuove genti. Ma non piacendo cotal interpretazione a Motezuma, Nezahualpilli lo sfidò al giuoco del pallone, ch' era frequentissimo anche fra gli stessi Re, e s' accordarono, che se il Re di Messico vinceva la partita, quello d' Acolhuacan rinunzierebbe alla sua interpretazione, stimandola falsa; ma se vinceva Nezahualpilli, Motezuma dovrebbe riconoscerla vera, ed abbracciarla. Sciocchezza veramente ridicola di quegli uomini nel credere dipendente la verità d' una predizione dalla destrezza del giuocatore, o dalla fortuna del giuoco; ma pure men perniciosa di quella degli antichi Europei, che compromettevano nella barbarie del duello, e nella incertezza delle armi la verità, l' innocenza, e l' onore. Restò Nezahualpilli vittorioso nel giuoco, e Motezuma sconsolato per la perdita, e per la confermazione di sì cattivo pronosticamento. Nondimeno volle tentare altra strada, sperando trovare una predizione più favorevole, che si contrappesasse con quella del Re d' Acolhuacan, e colla disgrazia del giuoco. Fece dunque consultar un famosissimo Astrologo, molto versato
e: a phenomenon, consulted his astrologers about it; but these not knowing how to divine its meaning, he asked it of the king of Bk. V. Acolhuacan, who was also given to astrology and divination. These kings, although they were related to each other and perpetually allied, did not however live in much harmony, ever since the king of Acolhuacan had put to death, as we shall soon see, his son Huexotzincatzin, heedless of the entreaties of Moctezuma, who, as uncle of that prince, had interceded for him. It had already been a long time since they had dealt with each other with that frequency and that confidence with which they used to; but this time the vain terror that weighed upon Moctezuma’s mind impelled him to avail himself of the learning of King Nezahualpilli; hence he begged him to come to Mexico to deliberate together on that matter, which pressed equally upon both. Nezahualpilli went, and after conferring at length with Moctezuma, was of the opinion, according to what the historians say, that the comet announced the future misfortunes of those kingdoms through the arrival of new peoples. But this interpretation not pleasing Moctezuma, Nezahualpilli challenged him to the ball game, which was very frequent even among the kings themselves, and they agreed that if the king of Mexico won the match, the king of Acolhuacan would renounce his interpretation, esteeming it false; but if Nezahualpilli won, Moctezuma should acknowledge it as true and embrace it. A truly ridiculous folly of those men, to believe that the truth of a prediction depended on the dexterity of the player or on the fortune of the game; but yet less pernicious than that of the ancient Europeans, who committed to the barbarity of the duel and the uncertainty of arms truth, innocence, and honor. Nezahualpilli remained victorious in the game, and Moctezuma disconsolate at the loss and at the confirmation of so evil a prognostication. Nevertheless he wished to try another way, hoping to find a more favorable prediction that might counterbalance that of the king of Acolhuacan and the misfortune at the game. He therefore had a most famous astrologer consulted, well versed

o: nelle superstizioni della Divinazione, colla quale avea renduto tanto celebre il suo nome in quella terra, ed erasi conciliata sì grande autorità, che senza uscir di casa era consultato come un oracolo dagli stessi Re. Egli sapendo senz' altro ciò ch' era avvenuto fra i due Re, in vece di dare una risposta gradevole al suo Sovrano, o almeno equivoca, come fanno per lo più tali pronosticatori, confermò la funesta predizione del Tezcucano. Sdegnossi tanto Motezuma della risposta, che in ricompensa fece rovinargli la casa, restando l' infelice indovino sepolto fra le rovine del suo santuario. Questi, ed altri simili pronosticamenti della caduta di quell' Imperio si vedono nelle pitture degli Americani, e nelle Storie degli Spagnuoli. Sono troppo lontano da persuadermi, che tutto ciò, che scritto troviamo sopra sì fatto argomento, degno sia della nostra fede; ma neppur si può dubitare della tradizione, che v' era fra gli Americani di dovere arrivare a quel regno delle nuove genti assai diverse da' proprj abitatori, che s' impadronirebbero di tutta la terra. Non v' è stata nel paese d' Anahuac veruna Nazion dirozzata, o mezzo dirozzata, che non abbia fatto fede di cotal tradizione, o colle loro testimonianze verbali, o colle proprie loro Storie. Non è possibile indovinare la prima origine di questa tradizione tanto universale; ma nel Secolo XV., ed anche nel XIV. dappoichè colla invenzione della bussola non temevano più gli uomini di perder di vista la terra, e gli Europei stimolati dall' ambizione, e dalla insaziabil fame dell' oro aveano cominciato a rendersi famigliari i perigli dell' Oceano, quel maligno spirito, capital nemico del genere umano, che gira incessantemente per tutta la terra spiando le azioni dei Mortali, potè facilmente congetturare i progressi degli Europei, la scoperta del nuovo Mondo, ed una parte de' grandi avvenimenti, che ivi erano per accadere: e non è inverisimile, che gli predicesse a Nazioni consacrate al suo culto, per confermarle colla stessa predizione dell' avvenire nella erronea persuasione della sua pretesa divinità. Ma se il Demonio pronosticava le future
e: in the superstitions of divination, by which he had made his name so Bk. V. celebrated in that land, and had won for himself such great authority that, without leaving his house, he was consulted like an oracle by the kings themselves. Knowing without any doubt what had passed between the two kings, instead of giving his sovereign a pleasing answer, or at least an equivocal one, as such prognosticators for the most part do, he confirmed the fatal prediction of the Texcocan. Moctezuma was so angered by the answer that, in recompense, he had his house pulled down, and the unfortunate diviner remained buried among the ruins of his sanctuary. These and other like prognostications of the fall of that empire are to be seen in the paintings of the Americans and in the histories of the Spaniards. I am far from persuading myself that everything we find written on such a subject is worthy of our belief; but neither can one doubt the tradition that existed among the Americans, that there were to arrive in that kingdom new peoples very different from its own inhabitants, who would take possession of the whole land. There was no civilized or half-civilized nation in the country of Anahuac that did not bear witness to this tradition, either by their verbal testimony or by their own histories. It is not possible to guess the first origin of so universal a tradition; but in the fifteenth century, and even in the fourteenth, after the invention of the compass had freed men from the fear of losing sight of land, and the Europeans, spurred on by ambition and by the insatiable hunger for gold, had begun to make the perils of the Ocean familiar to themselves, that malignant spirit, the capital enemy of mankind, who goes ceaselessly about the whole earth spying on the actions of mortals, could easily conjecture the progress of the Europeans, the discovery of the New World, and a part of the great events that were to take place there; and it is not improbable that he predicted them to nations consecrated to his worship, in order to confirm them, by that same prediction of the future, in the erroneous persuasion of his pretended divinity. Her Mexican princess. funeral was celebrated with a magnificence corresponding to the splendor of her birth, the king her brother and all the Mexican and Tlatelolca nobility attending. Her body was buried in a subterranean cave or grotto that was in the garden of the same palace, near a pond where she used to bathe, and the entrance of the cave was closed with a stone of no great weight. The following day a little girl of five or six years took it into her head to go from her mother’s apartment to that of the deceased’s steward, which lay on the other side of the garden, and in passing she saw the princess seated on the steps of the pond, and heard herself called by her with the word Cocoton, (f) which they use in speaking tenderly to children. The little girl, not being capable at her age of reflecting on the death of the princess, and thinking that she had come to bathe, as she was accustomed to do, approached without fear, and the princess sent her to call the wife of her steward. She went to call her; but the woman, smiling and caressing her, said to her: “My daughter, Papantzin is already dead, and yesterday we buried her.” But as the girl insisted, and even pulled her by the huepilli, or woman’s shift, she, more to please her than because she believed

Mexico on a clear night, without its cause ever being guessed, and in the preceding year so rapid and so extraordinary an agitation of the waters of the lake that it ruined some houses of Mexico, there being neither wind, nor earthquake, nor any other natural cause to which so rare a phenomenon could be ascribed. It is said also that in 1511 armed men were seen represented in the air, fighting among themselves and killing one another. These and other like phenomena, related by Acosta, by Torquemada, and by others, were found exactly described in the Mexican and Acolhua histories. Nor is it improbable that God, having announced by such prodigies the destruction of some cities, as is known to us partly from Holy Scripture and partly from the testimony of Josephus, of Eusebius of Caesarea, of Orosius, and of other authors, should employ the same providence in the general overthrow of an entire world, which is without doubt the rarest and most notable event of all those that are read of in human histories. The consternation caused in the mind of Moctezuma by such dismal presages did not turn him from thoughts of war. Many expeditions

e: loss of only ninety-five men they took one thousand three hundred Bk. V. and thirty-two prisoners, who were also brought to Mexico. With these and other conquests made in the three following years the Mexican empire attained its greatest extent, five or six years before its ruin, to which these same rapid conquests contributed greatly. Every province, every place conquered became a new enemy of the conquerors, which, impatient of the yoke to which it was not accustomed, and irritated by the violence, awaited nothing but some good occasion to avenge itself and to restore itself to its former liberty. The happiness of a kingdom does not consist in the extent of its dominions, nor even in the multitude of its vassals; indeed it never approaches its end so closely as when, by reason of its vast and immoderate extent, it can maintain neither the necessary union among its parts nor the vigor that is needed to resist the multitude of its enemies. Nor did the revolutions that occurred at this same time in the kingdom of Acolhuacan, caused by the death of King Nezahualpilli, § 15. contribute less to the ruin of the Mexican empire. After six months of this private life he returned to the capital, ordered his dear Xocotzin to withdraw with her children to the palace called Tecpilpan, and shut himself up in the one that was his ordinary residence, without letting himself be seen by anyone save some of his confidants, with the design of concealing his death in imitation of his father. In fact neither the time nor the other circumstances of his death were ever known. It is known only that he died in 1516, and that before dying he commanded the confidants whom he employed to burn his body secretly. Hence it came about that the common people, and even a good many nobles, remained persuaded that he was not dead, but had gone to the kingdom of Amaquemecan, whence his ancestors had their origin, as he had often said he wished to do. This king was of the same opinion in matters of religion as his great father Nezahualcoyotl. He despised in his mind the worship of idols, although outwardly he conformed with the people. He likewise imitated his father in zeal for the laws and in severity of justice, of which he gave a rare example in the last years of his reign. There was a law that forbade, under pain of death, the speaking of indecent words in the royal palace. This law was violated by one of the princes his sons, named Huexotzincatzin, whom he loved more than all the others, no less for his character and for the virtues that were already shining in his youth than for his being the first-born among the sons he had by his favorite Xocotzin; but the prince’s words had been rather the effect of youthful thoughtlessness than of any wicked purpose. The king learned of it from one of his concubines, to whom such words had been said. He asked her whether this had occurred before other persons, and, having learned that the prince’s tutors had been present, he withdrew to an apartment of the palace that was set aside for occasions of mourning. There he had the tutors summoned to examine them. They, fearing

The whole court was dismayed at so rigorous a sentence; the nobility interceded with prayers and tears, and the prince’s own mother, trusting in the great love the king bore her, presented herself to him weeping, and, to move him the more to compassion, brought her children with her. But neither reasons, nor prayers, nor tears sufficed to bend the king. “My son,” he said, “has violated the law. If I pardon him, it will be said that the laws are not made for everyone. Let my subjects know that to no one will transgression be pardoned, since I do not pardon it in the son whom I love most.” The queen, pierced by the keenest grief and despairing of being able to overcome the king’s firmness, said to him: “Since for so slight a cause you have driven from your heart all the affections of a father and of a husband, and wish to make yourself the executioner of your own son, what is left to you but to give death also to me and to these tender princes whom I have borne you?” The king then, with a grave look, commanded her to withdraw, since there was no longer any remedy. The queen went away disconsolate to her apartment, and there, in the company of some ladies who went to console her, abandoned herself to weeping. Meanwhile those who were charged with the prince’s execution kept delaying, so that, with time, zeal for justice being relaxed, there might be room for paternal love and for clemency; but the king, perceiving their intention, commanded that it be carried out at once, as in fact it was, to the general sorrow of the whole kingdom, and to the very great displeasure of King Moctezuma, not only because of the kinship that he had with the prince, but also because the entreaties he had interposed that the sentence be revoked had been disregarded.

o: sentenza. Poi che fu eseguito il supplizio, si rinchiuse il Re dentro una sala per lo spazio di quaranta giorni, senza lasciarsi veder da nessuno, per dare ivi tutto lo sfogo al suo dolore, e fece chiuder con muro le porte dell' appartamento del suo figliuolo, per levarsi dagli occhj quell' incentivo di cordoglio. Questa severità nel punire i trasgressori si contrappesava colla compassione, che mostrava, della miseria de' suoi sudditi. V' era nel suo palagio una finestra, che guardava la piazza del mercato, coperta da una gelosìa, donde osservava senza esser veduto, la gente che vi concorreva; e quando vedeva qualche donna mal vestita, la faceva chiamare, ed informatosi della vita di lei, e della sua necessità, la provvedeva del bisognevole per lei, e per tutti i suoi figliuoli, se gli aveva. Ogni giorno faceva nel suo palagio delle limosine a tutti gl'invalidi, ed orfanneli. V' era in Tezcuco un Ospedale per tutti quelli, che nella guerra aveano perduti gli occhi, o in qualunque altra maniera s' erano resi inutili per l' esercizio delle armi, ed ivi erano a spese del Re sostentati secondo la lor condizione, e spesse volte dallo stesso Re visitati. In cotali opere spendeva una gran parte delle sue rendite. L' ingegno di questo Re è stato assai celebrato dagli Storici di quel regno. Egli si propose da imitare e per gli studj, e per la condotta della vita lo esempio di suo Padre, ed in fatti gli fu assai somigliante. Con lui si può dir finita la gloria de' Re Cicimechi; poichè la discordia eccitatasi fra i suoi figliuoli diminuì lo splendor della Corte, indebolì le forze dello Stato, e lo dispose alla sua ultima rovina. Non dichiarò Nezahualpilli chi dovea succedergli nella Corona, come aveano fatto tutti i suoi Antecessori. Ignoriamo pure il motivo d' una tal trascuratezza, che fu sì perniciosa al regno di Acolhuacan. [margin: §. 16. Rivoluzioni del regno d' Acolhuacan.] Tosto che il Consiglio supremo del Re defunto fu assicurato della sua morte, si credette in obbligo d' eleggere il successore ad imitazione de' Messicani. Radunaronsi dunque per deliberare sopra un affare di tanto rilievo, e
e: After the execution had been carried out, the king shut himself up in Bk. V. a hall for the space of forty days, without letting himself be seen by anyone, in order to give full vent there to his grief, and he had the doors of his son’s apartment walled up, so as to remove from his eyes that incentive to sorrow. This severity in punishing transgressors was counterbalanced by the compassion that he showed for the misery of his subjects. There was in his palace a window that looked on the marketplace, covered by a lattice, from which he observed, without being seen, the people who gathered there; and when he saw some poorly dressed woman he had her called, and, having informed himself of her way of life and of her need, he provided her with what was necessary for her and for all her children, if she had any. Every day he gave alms in his palace to all the infirm and the orphans. There was in Texcoco a hospital for all those who in war had lost their eyes, or in any other way had been made useless for the exercise of arms, and there they were maintained at the king’s expense according to their condition, and often visited by the king himself. On such works he spent a great part of his revenues. The intelligence of this king has been much celebrated by the historians of that kingdom. He proposed to himself to imitate, both in his studies and in his conduct of life, the example of his father, and in fact he was very like him. With him the glory of the Chichimec kings may be said to have ended; for the discord that arose among his sons diminished the splendor of the court, weakened the forces of the state, and disposed it to its final ruin. Nezahualpilli did not declare who was to succeed him on the throne, as all his predecessors had done. We likewise do not know the motive of such negligence, which proved so pernicious to the kingdom of Acolhuacan.                        § 16. As soon as the supreme council of the deceased king was assured Revolutions of the of his death, it believed itself obliged to elect the successor in imita‐ kingdom of Acolhuacan. tion of the Mexicans. They therefore assembled to deliberate upon an affair of such moment, and beginning

o: cominciando a discorrere il più anziano, e più autorevole di loro; rappresentò i gravissimi danni, che potrebbe recar allo stato l' Anarchìa, se si ritardava l' elezione: che egli era di parere, che dovesse ricader la corona nel Principe Cacamatzin; poichè oltre alla sua prudenza, ed al suo coraggio, era il primogenito della prima Principessa Messicana, che sposò il defunto Re. Tutti gli altri consiglieri aderirono a questo parere, che era tanto giusto, e di una persona tanto autorevole. I Principi, che in una sala vicina aspettavano la risoluzione del Consiglio, furono pregati d' entrarvi per sentirla. Entrati che furono tutti, si diede la principal sedia a Cacamatzin, ch' era giovane di venti due anni, ed a' fianchi di lui sedettero i suoi fratelli Coanacotzin di venti, e Ixtlilxochitl di diciannove anni. Alzossi poi quell' Anziano ch' era stato il primo a parlare, e dichiarò la risoluzione del Consiglio, nella quale era compromessa quella del regno, di dar la Corona a Cacamatzin atteso il diritto della primogenitura. Ixtlilxochitl, ch' era un giovane ambizioso ed intraprendente, si oppose dicendo, che se il Re fosse stato veramente morto, avrebbe senz' altro nominato il successore: che il non averlo fatto era indizio non dubbioso della sua vita, ed essendo vivo il legittimo Sovrano, era attentato ne' sudditi il nominare un successore. I Consiglieri conoscendo bene l' indole d' Ixtlilxochitl, non osarono contraddirgli apertamente; ma pregarono Coanacotzin di dire il suo sentimento. Questo Principe lodò, e confermò la determinazione del Consiglio, ed accennò gl' inconvenienti, ch' erano per avvenire, se si ritardasse la esecuzione. Ixtlilxochitl gli contraddisse, tacciandolo di leggerezza, e d' inconsiderazione, mentre non s' accorgeva, che nell' abbracciar tal partito favoriva i disegni di Motezuma, ch' era troppo inclinato a Cacamatzin, e si adoperava per metterlo sul trono, sperando aver in costui un Re di cera, a cui dar potesse qualunque forma gli piacesse. „ Non è ragionevole, o mio fratello, replicò Coanacotzin, l' opporsi ad una risoluzione sì savia e sì giusta. Non avvertite, che quando non fosse Re Cacamatzin,
e: to speak, the oldest and most authoritative of them set forth the very Bk. V. grave harms that anarchy could bring upon the state if the election were delayed: that he was of the opinion that the crown should fall to Prince Cacamatzin; since, besides his prudence and his courage, he was the first-born of the first Mexican princess whom the deceased king had married. All the other councilors adhered to this opinion, which was so just, and was that of so authoritative a person. The princes, who were awaiting in a neighboring hall the resolution of the council, were asked to enter in order to hear it. When all had entered, the principal seat was given to Cacamatzin, who was a young man of twenty-two years, and at his sides sat his brothers Coanacochtzin, of twenty, and Ixtlilxochitl, of nineteen years. Then that elder who had been the first to speak rose, and declared the resolution of the council, in which that of the kingdom was pledged, to give the crown to Cacamatzin by reason of the right of primogeniture. Ixtlilxochitl, who was an ambitious and enterprising young man, opposed it, saying that if the king had really been dead he would doubtless have named his successor; that his not having done so was an unmistakable sign that he was alive, and that, the lawful sovereign being alive, it was a presumption on the part of the subjects to name a successor. The councilors, knowing well the disposition of Ixtlilxochitl, did not dare to contradict him openly; but they begged Coanacochtzin to say what he thought. This prince praised and confirmed the determination of the council, and pointed out the inconveniences that were to follow if the execution were delayed. Ixtlilxochitl contradicted him, charging him with levity and thoughtlessness, since he did not perceive that in embracing such a course he favored the designs of Moctezuma, who was too much inclined toward Cacamatzin, and was working to put him on the throne, hoping to have in him a king of wax, to whom he could give whatever form he pleased. “It is not reasonable, my brother,” replied Coanacochtzin, “to oppose so wise and so just a resolution. Do you not observe that if Cacamatzin were not king,

o: a me, non a voi si dovrebbe la Corona? „ „ E' vero, disse allora Ixtlilxochitl, che se per la successione si debbe considerar soltanto l' età, la Corona si debbe a Cacamatzin, e mancando lui, a voi; ma se si ha riguardo, siccome è giusto, al coraggio, a me è dovuta, piuttosto che a voi, ovvero a Cacamatzin. „ I Consiglieri vedendo, che la collera de' Principi s' andava vieppiù riscaldando, imposero silenzio a tutti e due, e licenziarono la radunanza. I due Principi andarono alla lor Madre la Regina Xocotzin, per continuar la loro contesa, e Cacamatzin accompagnato da molta Nobiltà si portò subito a Messico per informar Motezuma di ciò, che era avvenuto, e per addimandare il suo ajuto. Motezuma, il quale oltre all' amor, che gli portava, vedeva il dritto di tal Principe, ed il consenso della Nazione, gli consigliò di metter in salvo prima d' ogni altra cosa il Real tesoro, e gli promise d' accomodar la lite col suo fratello, e d' impiegar l' armi Messicane in favor di lui, se mai non fossero abbastanza le negoziazioni. Ixtlilxochitl tosto che seppe la partenza di Cacamatzin, ed antivide le conseguenze del ricorso di lui a Motezuma, uscì dalla Corte con tutti i suoi partigiani, e se n' andò agli stati, che aveano i suoi Ai nelle montagne di Meztitlan. Coanacotzin diede prontamente avviso a Cacamatzin, acciocchè senza indugio si restituisse a Tezcuco, e si prevalesse di sì opportuna occasione per incoronarsi. Pigliò Cacamatzin il salutevole consiglio del suo fratello, e portossi a quella Corte accompagnato da Cuitlahuazin, fratello di Motezuma, e Signor d' Iztapalapan, e da molta Nobiltà Messicana. Cuitlahuatzin, senza perder tempo, convocò la Nobiltà Tezcucana nell' Hueitecpan, o sia gran palagio de' Re d' Acolhuacan, e gli presentò il Principe Cacamatzin, acciocchè fosse da loro riconosciuto per legittimo Sovrano. Accettaronlo tutti, e restò allora determinato il giorno per la solennità dell' Incoronazione; ma s' impedì colle nuove, che arrivarono alla Corte, che il Principe Ixtlilxochitl scendeva dalle montagne di Meztitlan alla testa d' un grosso esercito,
e: to me, not to you, would the crown be due?” “It is true,” said Ixtlilxochitl then, “that if in the succession only age is to be consid‐ Bk. V. ered, the crown is due to Cacamatzin, and, he failing, to you; but if regard is had, as is just, to courage, it is due to me rather than to you or to Cacamatzin.” The councilors, seeing that the anger of the princes was growing ever hotter, imposed silence on both and dismissed the assembly. The two princes went to their mother, Queen Xocotzin, to continue their dispute, and Cacamatzin, accompanied by many nobles, went at once to Mexico to inform Moctezuma of what had happened and to ask his help. Moctezuma, who, besides the love he bore him, saw the right of that prince and the consent of the nation, advised him to place in safety, before anything else, the royal treasure, and promised him to settle the quarrel with his brother, and to employ the Mexican arms in his favor if negotiations should not prove sufficient. As soon as Ixtlilxochitl learned of the departure of Cacamatzin, and foresaw the consequences of his recourse to Moctezuma, he left the court with all his partisans, and went off to the domains that his tutors had in the mountains of Metztitlan. Coanacochtzin promptly gave notice to Cacamatzin to return without delay to Texcoco, and to take advantage of so opportune an occasion to be crowned. Cacamatzin took the salutary counsel of his brother, and went to that court accompanied by Cuitláhuac, brother of Moctezuma and lord of Iztapalapan, and by many Mexican nobles. Cuitláhuac, without losing time, convoked the Texcocan nobility in the Hueitecpan, or great palace of the kings of Acolhuacan, and presented to them Prince Cacamatzin, that he might be recognized by them as lawful sovereign. All accepted him, and the day was then fixed for the ceremony of the coronation; but it was prevented by the news that arrived at the court, that Prince Ixtlilxochitl was descending from the mountains of Metztitlan at the head of a large army,

o: Questo inquieto giovane subito che arrivò a Meztitlan, convocò tutti i Signori de' luoghi situati in quelle grandi montagne, e lor fece sapere il suo disegno d' opporsi a suo statello Cacamatzin sotto pretesto di zelo per l' onore, e per la libertà delle Nazioni Cicimeca, ed Acolhua: ch' era cosa indegna ed assai pericolosa l' ubbidire ad un Re sì pieghevole alla volontà di quello di Messico: che i Messicani dimenticatisi di quanto dovevano agli Acolhui, volevano aumentar le loro inique usurpazioni con quella del regno d' Acolhuacan: ch' egli dalla sua parte era determinato di adoperare tutto il coraggio, che Iddio gli avea dato, nel difender la sua patria dalla tirannìa di Motezuma. Con sì fatte ragioni suggeritegli verisimilmente da' suoi Ai, riscaldò in tal maniera gli animi di quei Signori, che tutti s' esibirono ad ajutarlo con tutte le loro forze, ed in fatti levarono tante truppe, che quando il Principe scese dalle montagne, montava il suo esercito, per quel che dicono, a più di cento mila uomini. In tutti i luoghi dove passava era ben accolto, o per paura della sua possanza, o per inclinazione a favorir le sue pretensioni. Da Tepepolco mandò un' ambasciata agli Otompanesi, ordinando loro di prestare a lui ubbidienza, come a lor proprio Re; ma costoro risposero, che morto il Re Nezahualpilli, altro Padrone non riconoscevano, che Cacamatzin, il quale era stato pacificamente accettato nella Corte, e si trovava già in possesso del trono d' Acolhuacan. Questa risposta irritò Ixtlilxochitl, e lo fece andar precipitosamente contra quella Città. Gli Otompanesi gli vennero all' incontro in ordine di battaglia; ma benchè facessero qualche resistenza all' esercito nemico, furono pur vinti, e presa dal Principe la loro Città. Tra i morti cadde lo stesso Signor d' Otompan, e ciò appunto anticipò al Principe la vittoria. Questo successo mise in grande inquietudine Cacamatzin, e tutta la sua Corte: onde temendo, che volesse anche il nemico assediar la capitale, procurò fortificarsi; ma il Principe contento di vedersi rispettato e temuto, non si
e: This restless young man, as soon as he arrived at Metztitlan, conBk. V. voked all the lords of the places situated in those great mountains, and made known to them his design of opposing his brother Cacamatzin, under the pretext of zeal for the honor and liberty of the Chichimec and Acolhua nations: that it was an unworthy and very dangerous thing to obey a king so pliant to the will of him of Mexico; that the Mexicans, forgetting how much they owed to the Acolhuas, wished to add to their iniquitous usurpations that of the kingdom of Acolhuacan; that he for his part was determined to employ all the courage that God had given him in defending his country from the tyranny of Moctezuma. With such reasons, suggested to him probably by his tutors, he so inflamed the minds of those lords that all offered to help him with all their forces, and in fact they raised so many troops that, when the prince came down from the mountains, his army amounted, by what they say, to more than a hundred thousand men. In all the places through which he passed he was well received, either from fear of his power or from inclination to favor his pretensions. From Tepepulco he sent an embassy to the people of Otompan, ordering them to render him obedience as to their own king; but they answered that, King Nezahualpilli being dead, they recognized no other master than Cacamatzin, who had been peacefully accepted in the capital and was already in possession of the throne of Acolhuacan. This answer irritated Ixtlilxochitl, and made him march headlong against that city. The people of Otompan came out to meet him in battle order; but although they offered some resistance to the enemy army, they were nevertheless defeated, and their city was taken by the prince. Among the dead fell the lord of Otompan himself, and this very circumstance hastened the victory for the prince. This occurrence put Cacamatzin and all his court in great disquiet; whence, fearing that the enemy might wish even to besiege the capital, he sought to fortify himself; but the prince, content to see himself respected and feared, did not move

o: mosse allora da Otompan; ma dispose delle guardie sulle strade coll' ordine di non far male a nessuno, di non impedire il passo a' particolari, che dalla Corte volessero andare a qualunque altro luogo, e di ossequiar le persone di primo rango, che vi passassero. Cacamatzin vedendo le forze, e la risoluzione del fratello, e stimando manco male il sacrificar una parte, benchè grande del regno, che il perderlo tutto, gli mandò col consenso di Coanacotzin un' ambasciata per far con esso lui qualche accomodamento. Mandò a dirgli, che ritenesse pure, se voleva, tutti i dominj delle montagne; poichè egli si contentava della Corte, e degli stati delle pianure: che voleva anche partire col suo fratello Coanacotzin le rendite del regno; ma insieme lo pregava di lasciar ogni altra pretensione, e di non perturbar più la pubblica tranquillità. Gli Ambasciatori furono due Personaggi del sangue Reale d' Acolhuacan, a cui portava un gran rispetto Ixtlilxochitl. Questo Principe rispose, che i suoi fratelli potevano far tutto ciò che lor piacesse: che a lui era caro, che Cacamatzin fosse in possessione del regno d' Acolhuacan: ch' egli niente macchinava contro loro, nè contro lo stato: che non manteneva per altro quell' esercito, che per opporsi agli ambiziosi disegni de' Messicani, i quali aveano recati de' gravissimi disgusti, e de' sospetti a suo Padre Nezahualpilli: che se allora si divideva il regno pel comun interesse della Nazione, sperava di vederlo un' altra volta unito: che soprattutto si guardassero di cadere ne' laccj dell' astuto Motezuma. Non s' ingannò pure Ixtlilxochitl nella diffidenza di Motezuma; poichè in fatti questo Re fu quegli, che diede lo sventurato Cacamatzin, come vedremo, in mano agli Spagnuoli, malgrado l' amor che gli portava. Coll' accordo fatto col fratello restò Cacamatzin nella pacifica possessione della corona d' Acolhuacan; ma co' suoi dominj troppo diminuiti: mentre ciò che avea ceduto, era una parte considerabile del regno. Ixtlilxochitl mantenne ognora le sue truppe in moto, e spesse volte si lasciò vedere col suo esercito nelle vicinanze di Messico, sfidando
e: then from Otompan; but he posted guards on the roads with orders Bk. V. to do harm to no one, not to hinder the passage of private persons who might wish to go from the capital to any other place, and to show respect to persons of the first rank who might pass there. Cacamatzin, seeing the forces and the resolution of his brother, and thinking it a lesser evil to sacrifice a part, though a large one, of the kingdom than to lose it all, sent him, with the consent of Coanacochtzin, an embassy to make some accommodation with him. He sent to tell him that he might keep, if he wished, all the dominions of the mountains, since he himself was content with the capital and the states of the plains; that he wished also to share with his brother Coanacochtzin the revenues of the kingdom; but at the same time he begged him to renounce every other pretension and to disturb no more the public tranquillity. The ambassadors were two personages of the royal blood of Acolhuacan, for whom Ixtlilxochitl had great respect. This prince replied that his brothers might do whatever they pleased; that it was pleasing to him that Cacamatzin should be in possession of the kingdom of Acolhuacan; that he was plotting nothing against them, nor against the state; that he maintained that army for no other purpose than to oppose the ambitious designs of the Mexicans, who had caused the gravest vexations and suspicions to his father Nezahualpilli; that if the kingdom was divided at that time for the common interest of the nation, he hoped to see it united again another time; that above all they should take care not to fall into the snares of the crafty Moctezuma. Nor was Ixtlilxochitl mistaken in his distrust of Moctezuma; for in fact that king was the very one who gave the unfortunate Cacamatzin, as we shall see, into the hands of the Spaniards, in spite of the love he bore him. By the agreement made with his brother, Cacamatzin remained in peaceful possession of the crown of Acolhuacan, but with his dominions much diminished, since what he had ceded was a considerable part of the kingdom. Ixtlilxochitl kept his troops always in motion, and often let himself be seen with his army in the neighborhood of Mexico, defying Moctezuma

o: Motezuma a combattere a corpo a corpo con lui. Ma questo Re non trovavasi più in istato di accettar una tale sfida: il fuoco ch' ebbe nella sua giovanezza s' era già cominciato a smorzare cogli anni, e le delizie dimestiche gli aveano indebolito l' animo: nè prudenza sarebbe stata lo esporsi ad un tal conflitto con un giovane sì risoluto, il quale con segrete negoziazioni avea già tirata al suo partito una gran parte delle Provincie Messicane. Nondimeno spesse volte combatterono i Messicani con quell' esercito, restando or vinti, or vittoriosi. In una di quelle zuffe fu preso un parente del Re di Messico, il quale era uscito alla guerra colla risoluzione di far prigione quel Principe, e condurlo legato a Messico, e così lo avea promesso a Motezuma. Seppe Ixtlilxochitl questa arrogante promessa, e per vendicarsi avendolo fatto legare e coprir di canna secca, lo fece bruciar vivo a vista di tutto l' esercito. Nel decorso della nostra storia faremo vedere, quanta parte ebbe questo inquieto Principe nella felicità degli Spagnuoli, i quali a questo tempo cominciarono a lasciarsi vedere sulle coste del Golfo Messicano; ma prima d' intraprendere la narrazione d' una guerra, che mise tutti que' regni in iscompiglio, è d' uopo far conoscere la Religione, il Governo, le arti, ed i costumi de' Messicani. Fine del Tomo Primo.
e: to fight hand to hand with him. But this king was no longer in a state Bk. V. to accept such a challenge: the fire that he had had in his youth had already begun to die down with the years, and domestic delights had weakened his spirit; nor would it have been prudent to expose himself to such a conflict with so resolute a young man, who by secret negotiations had already drawn to his side a great part of the Mexican provinces. Nevertheless the Mexicans often fought with that army, being now defeated, now victorious. In one of those skirmishes a relative of the king of Mexico was taken, who had gone out to the war with the resolution of making that prince prisoner and bringing him bound to Mexico, and had so promised Moctezuma. Ixtlilxochitl learned of this arrogant promise, and, to avenge himself, having had him bound and covered with dry cane, had him burned alive in sight of the whole army. In the course of our history we shall show how large a part this restless prince had in the good fortune of the Spaniards, who at this time began to let themselves be seen on the coasts of the Gulf of Mexico; but before undertaking the narration of a war that threw all those kingdoms into confusion, it is necessary to make known the religion, the government, the arts, and the customs of the Mexicans. End of the First Volume.
